title: Zack Grossi: ‘Mark Andrews is a Fun Guy to Coach’ | Baltimore Ravens
text: opportunity given me by Jesse, Mr. Bisciotti, and Eric DeCosta, and Ozzie Newsome. I don't take it lightly, and I'm excited to be here. Fire away. >> Zach, obviously the defense uh tight ends got two rookie draft picks. How would they look so far in training camp? >> Yeah, I thought what they did in the spring and then what they did with their bodies and strength can from a strength and conditioning standpoint in the summer allowed them to come into camp and put their best foot forward. They play fast. They know what to do. They're smart kids. They're wired the right way. They work hard at it. They prepare for practice the right way, and I thought that's allowed them to kind of show some of their natural skill sets early on cuz they're not playing slow. Uh pleased with the way those guys have approached things so far, and we got a long way to go. >> Mention long way to go. So, what else are you hoping to see from those two guys over the next two weeks? >> You know, it's I don't really think about what I'm hoping to see. We're just trying to We're trying to be process driven, worry about what do we have to do that day to get better. What do we What do we have to do for that practice? What's the next? The meetings, the recovery, whatever the next thing is, we give it all of our attention. Every play we give Every play has a life and history of its own. We're not too worried about big picture things right now. We just kind of got our nose down. We're grinding. We're installing the offense. We're learning technique. Everything that we're giving them, those young guys, is very foreign to them. They don't have a lot of experience with their college systems from what we're asking them to do. We're throwing a lot at them, and uh they're doing a good job. Like I said, just working, okay, keeping their head down, and uh not getting too worried about the results right now. >> What's it been like getting to know Getting to know and working with Mark Andrews? >> It's been unbelievable. Mark is a uh Mark is a fun guy to coach. He leads our room, his competitive nature, the way he prepares, the way he recovers, the way he attacks the day, the way he attacks the football, the way he attacks his Like I said, his recovery. He leads, he sets the tone for our group on a daily basis, and he's been an absolute joy to the Um he's been very receptive to things that um, I've given him and uh, he's been fun to work with every day. Like I said, leads our group, true pro, and uh, it's been an absolute joy so far. >> We know from DeCoud and Dwayne that blocking is going to be such an essential piece for this I mean, you consider you know, just blocking technique, blocking toughness, sort of the foundational piece for for like, "Hey, at a bare minimum, guys, we need you to be good in this area." >> I think that's the part for the young guys that is the most foreign to them, uh, based on what they had to do in college, based on what we're asking them to do. And that's the part where they're learning the most technique, fundamentals, all the different ways we make mic points, all the different way we ID runs. And uh, that's the part that I'm pleased with the way that they're attacking it and learning blocks, footwork, hand placement. It's all very different for them. And uh, look, you have to be able to block in this league, you know, as a tight end. You have to be able to um, win the C-gap, okay, all the all the different places that we put tight ends, okay, we put them on the ball, off the ball. We do two-back runs, okay, we line up on as receivers. We do perimeter schemes, okay, all all different types of uh, zone schemes, gap schemes, all kind of stuff. So, you have to be versatile and you have to be able to handle different types of blocks. We're not We don't have one-trick ponies and we're not looking for one-trick ponies in the run game. So, uh, that's how we're we're trying to develop those guys in all facets of blocking and obviously it's important to the success of our offense. >> What about Durham? I mean, Durham was obviously with Chicago last year, worked with DeCoud in that offense. How helpful is he when you have those teaching points with the younger guys? >> Yeah, Durham's been great. Durham was in Chicago last year, obviously, so he has some uh, base knowledge of of this offense, but he's also has 8 years before that in Miami with a bunch of different systems, a bunch of different offenses. He's been an absolute pro. Um, he's as steady as the day is long. He's consistent as it can be. He shows those young guys, you know, he teaches them about recovery. He teaches them about just kind of the ecosystem of the NFL, the ups and downs, and it's a long season, and you know, don't get don't get to don't ride the highs and ride the lows. And he does a really good job with those guys. Overall, I'm pleased the way the room has come together, right? Yeah, you know, Mark is the room is built around Mark, and everybody kind of complements him, and but those guys have done a good job connecting off the field, and Durham's been at the forefront of that, and I'm really, really pleased with him. He's a great addition to us with what he can do on the field, and off the field, he's been a a true pro and a joy to work with. >> All good? >> Thanks, guys. Thanks.

text: What's up everyone? >> Josh, um we're just talking to Zach about some of the teaching points that they've been going through with blocking and and you know, a college offense to an NFL offense almost is a big jump. Um what do you feel like you're most focused on in terms of kind of creating those run lanes and being a part of the run game as it's been mapped out for you? >> I think step number one is kind of actually knowing what to do. Um and really just kind of investing on why we're doing it and you know, who we're opening up the lane for and you know, what their run tendencies are, what kind of back we're having back there. Um but you know, coach Grossi is doing a great job kind of teaching that why and from then on you can kind of use your physicality and everything that you kind of preach during individual drill and stuff like that to use during team drills and stuff like that to really kind of work on your technique and stuff like that. So, yep. >> You know, I know really only Mark is the guy returning from last year's group, but you know, that tight end group sort of has a legacy of of being extra physical, especially in the blocking game. Um you know, how much do you feel like you're trying to live up to the standards set by previous teams in Baltimore? >> Yeah, absolutely. That's a that's a great question. I'm trying to embody that 100%. Um you know, coming out of college like um that summer of my senior year, uh I really kind of dove into the physicality and the the want to to block. And you know, now I've kind of grown into the player where I'm not afraid to put my head in there and you know, mess up on anything. So, um as long as I'm kind of giving 100% and actually touch somebody, then I'm fine with it. >> Mhm. >> What are you taking away from Mark Andrews to this point beyond what you knew about him as a player watching him in college? >> Yeah, at first, I mean, he was an intimidating guy to kind of go up to just cuz of the I mean, the legacy he has and what he's done for the city of Baltimore and this team. But like kind of getting to know the guy and really diving into his mind during the game and you know, bouncing ideas off one another during routes and you know, whenever we come back to the huddle and it's like, "Hey, you're lining up here, you're lining up there." And it's just bouncing ideas off one another and I mean, I'm just as a rookie just being a sponge to everything he has to teach me and it's working out great. >> How helpful is it to have another rookie kind of going through the same learning curve as you are in the same room? >> Oh, it's awesome. I mean, Matt and and Ty, we're all kind of you know, in this together and really just kind of going through everything that's being thrown at us left and right and I mean, it's been said before by coach Doyle like they're giving us a lot of stuff really quickly. And going from that college offense to NFL offense, like it can get pretty overwhelming. But knowing you have somebody there to kind of confide in and be you like, "You know what? What do we have on this play?" And you know, "Are you sure we have this and that?" And then we'll go back into the notes that we've taken and really kind of get that cleared up. But you know, having that other person in there along the way along the journey like it's it's been it's been awesome. >> Josh, what do you feel like you've learned the most up to this point in training camp and what are you hoping to show during the preseason? >> You know, in the detail of everything that we do. Really just kind of on the field and alignments and stuff and you know, even motions. Just kind of knowing how bad that kind of messes up defense defenses and how that can quickly change the schematics of everything. And so I think the detail in everything that we do even from inside the building. Just kind of from like recovery and things like that, it can give you any edge that you can get on your opponent, it's worth taking. >> Josh, when you got drafted you I guess the like the hope was that you'd be around here for a long, long time. But do you kind of go into preseason feeling like there's a job to be won on the 53-man the and that you put that kind of pressure on yourself? >> Um if I'm being honest, no. I'm not. Um I knew kind of going into this I was going to be two older guys in the room. Um but my biggest goal was kind of getting that understanding of what I'm doing and where I'm at. Um knowing that there is a legacy where for the tight ends here in Baltimore. Um you know, you can't just expect to come in as a rookie and be the big top dog. Like you can't you can't do that. Um especially being behind people with so much experience like Mark Andrews and Durham Smythe. Like you can't do that. So my entire goal was just kind of getting an understanding of the offense that coach Doyles teaching and preaching and having coach Grassi kind of giving me little tips and helpful ideas along the way to really get me to understand everything. >> Josh, a lot of tight ends have made their careers on blocking. Durham is one of those guys. What have you learned from him specifically when it comes to blocking so? >> I mean when it comes to blocking, I mean he's he's a statue. I mean when it comes to that and I mean just knowing that you can kind of go back and watch his tape and everything is so consistent and he's a very consistent guy to learn behind and you know, just the way he uses his base whenever he's blocking, the way he strikes his hands and using leverage and using everything against the defender that he can just to win blocks and um I wouldn't say he's the biggest like the biggest dude out there. Not like a Pat Ricard or anything like that who's who we've uh are all familiar with but um I mean he holds his own and but he's smart about it. And he's super consistent. So anything that I can take from from base, striking, things like that. I want to do that. >> And then off the field, how has he helped you get used to the NFL? >> Yeah, I I ask him kind of every day. I'm like, "Hey man, like does it get easier?" Cuz he's been in this offense before. Um and he kind of just reassures me like, "Yeah." Gives me tips on remembering plays and um just things like that. Little little niches here and there in the game and I mean just that off the field stuff. Even some recovery, too. Like I see him recovery. He's there 6:00 in the morning. sometimes even 5:30. Like he's there in the morning. He's a great like example to kind of learn from. >> Josh, >> Yeah, absolutely. Aussie and I talk all the time. Like he's he's a good guy. Whenever we pass each other, dab each other up, roll tide, man. Like that's what it is. B City 5 brothers for life. But yeah, I'd say so. >> Josh, obviously, you know, you're a Bama boy. I'm an alum from Alabama. Can you just talk about that culture, you know, what that represents, and how the Ravens is maybe maybe similar or different as far as culture and expectations? >> Yeah, as soon as so as soon as I got to the South and got to Alabama, like you kind of felt that heaviness in your chest of what Alabama football was as soon as you walk into the building. You walk in to the right, there's massive signs with all the championships on there. SEC championship, national championship. So you kind of go in there knowing what you have and what standard you need to uphold. Um so that's like something that we took it took pride in every single day and work worked hard towards. And I mean you kind of feel that here also. It's I mean even when I'm out exploring in the city, you know, you kind of feel that um that heaviness of what like the flock is all about and the city of Baltimore and the sports culture that surrounds football. Um you kind of feel the same um energy and heftiness that it has. >> Two more? >> Um yeah, for sure. There's been times where um I've doubted really kind of knowing everything that needs to be going on. Um but you know, talking to other guys, like it's just reassurance after reassurance of, you know, like not every single play is going to be, you know, ran during practice. So um I mean we have scripted plays and that's where it's great having another rookie kind of going through it. Um kind of bouncing ideas off of Matt and off of Ty, and just even Durham or Mark. Like I know Mark's learning this for the first time as well. So, we're all kind of moving through this and um but you know, yeah, there has been times where it's been tough, but it's football. That's what it is. It's what a massive playbook will give you. >> Josh, how does the verbage here compare to what you were doing at Alabama? >> Yeah, uh it's it's pretty similar in terms of what we were running. I know coach Grub coming at off of that uh I believe it was that 2024 season um with the Seahawks. Uh he kind of brought some pro style offenses to that 2025 Alabama team. And just kind of the verbage of everything that he's using from combo blocks with the with the tackles to I mean routes. I mean anything like that just little verbage here and I mean some of the coaches will use it here and I'll be like, "Hey, I've I've heard that word before." And it's um and honestly, I'm I'm grateful for that that coach Grub actually had that experience and kind of brought it to Alabama. Um especially my senior year just so it made that transition going to the NFL a little bit easier. >> Thanks, guys. >> Appreciate you.

title: Durham Smythe: ‘Declan Doyle is Built for This’ | Baltimore Ravens
text: Hayden, as a guy who's, you know, Josh was just talking about how how impressed he's been by your blocking and and Katie Seen a great guy. Yeah, just using your physicality in offense. That being said, coming to Baltimore, um what kind of um respect you have for the standard that's been set here, especially in the tight end >> Yeah, a ton of respect. I think I mentioned it a couple months ago in the podcast they do here, but this organization is synonymous with physicality and you know, the AFC North is, you know, one of the most physical divisions in the history of football. So, yeah, even like playing against the Ravens the last 9 years, it's like, all right, no matter how much talent they have, it's going to be a physical game. So, I think you uh when when I come in, like that's something you think about. I have a ton of respect for, like you mentioned, the lineage of tight ends that have come through here. Um I remember growing up and watching, you know, Todd Heap and Dennis Pitta and those guys and obviously Mark has been one of the best tight ends in the NFL for a decade now here. Um so, it it's it's it's awesome to be a part of, honestly. >> What's it been like seeing Todd Monken in this system where, you know, he's running the show, whereas last year in Chicago, I know he's a coordinator, but Ben Johnson was calling the plays. >> Yeah, I mean, he's he's built for this. Obviously, he's he's rose pretty quickly in in this field, but it's it's deserving. Um you could see that last year. Obviously, Ben's calling the plays, but but Todd Monken is is is right there knowing what to do. He could have called plays if he needed to. He's he's built for this. Um he's been around some great offensive minds in the last decade. Um and now he's kind of making um all of those his own thing. It's pretty exciting and uh I'm I'm excited to work with him. >> When you have two rookies in the tight end room, especially in your They're looking to you to be like, "Hey, help me make sense of this." >> How how has it been adapting to that role where you're kind of not only playing but teaching? >> Yeah, I mean, I've been around, you know, a lot of rookies now um in the last 7 or 8 years and um I think the thing that jumps out about the guys that we have in our room this year is just how eager they are to learn. Um not only from, you know, Mark, myself, but just, you know, the entire offense from a holistic standpoint. Um so, that's really cool to see. Obviously, they're very talented players and uh and really good guys. I I I say that, too. You know, when you come in when rookies come in, you're always like, "All right, well, I'm going to have to work with this these guys for, you know, 8 months, so hopefully they're cool people." Uh and and they are. So, I think they really are a combination of a lot of great things. Uh yeah, I mean, I think so. I think the way he teaches the game, um whether it be in installs, techniques, I think it's just very clear. Um so, when someone is very clear about what they want, why we're doing what we're doing, um it it it gives you a holistic view of the offense. You understand why we're doing what we're doing. Um and I think that can slow the game down for a lot of people. I think that's for the last 2 years, that's that's really helped me. Um when you know it from a from a holistic standpoint, you you understand the offense and and everything slows down a little bit. Yeah, I mean, I I didn't really see it or, you know, what happened. Um but that's, you know, training camp is um you know part of it is a battle of attrition always cuz it's a two-sided sword. Obviously we have to get our work in you have to get calloused up for the season. And then you know sometimes things like that are going to happen which you know obviously are unfortunate. And again I don't know anything about it. So you know hopefully he's okay. Um but yeah that's kind of how it goes. >> You know you've worked in some some really good offenses including one last year. Lamar Jackson and and Derrick Henry are both such unique runners in the NFL and obviously in very unique ways. What's it like kind of getting used to kind of feel getting a feel for where they're going to go or how they're going to run behind you while you block? >> I mean I think first and foremost it's obviously any play during any season you want to get your job done. That's the name of the game. You have to do your job. But when you have Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry behind you there's almost a part of you that's like I'm not going to let that guy down. You know a guy who's won two MVPs and could probably have four at this point and then the best modern era maybe on the pace to be the best running back of all time behind you. I think something in your mind is like all right I'm going to do this maybe not harder but I'm going to do it to literally the best of my ability for that those guys. So I think it's it's it's wild to be a part of it. I'm I'm honored to be you know blocking for those guys. And obviously through training camp you get a feel for how they run and you know you definitely want to stay out of Derrick's way because that that that's a big man moving really fast. So we'll say about that. >> As an as an extended play threat a lot of Lamar's circle's value is extended plays and what he does on that. Have you gotten a sense of where you need to go to where he is on the play when he is under pressure? >> Yeah obviously that's one of his uh elite skills among many. Um And yes there is a method to the madness. I think uh uh Declan's done a very good job of learning. Um I think last year helped too because um our quarterback in Chicago was was very good at escaping the pocket as well. So, I think they've kind of come up with a uh a little bit of a formula of a method to the scramble drill. Um I think it's very effective. Obviously, at the end of the day you're just making a play when that happens, but it is good to have, you know, some parameters. Um and uh I think they've done a great job of of trying to teach that over the last couple months. Yeah, I mean I I think the way this offense is taught, whether it be, you know, last year in Chicago, this year here, you you kind of want to stress the players as much as possible, as fast as possible. So, at the beginning of of teaching things, it can be a little rough cuz there's so much information um thrown at you at once, but I think over the longevity of the season, which you kind of saw with us last year in Chicago, we started a little slow and then everything caught on at once. Obviously, we're on a race to to, you know, master it faster than that. I think that's what this game is, especially when there's a new offense or a new scheme being installed. It's a race to master it across the board as fast as possible to get into, you know, your flow state as soon as the season starts. Um and I think, you know, we're coming around to that. Obviously, there's a lot to work on um in that regard, but we're definitely in a race in the next 3 weeks. Appreciate it.

title: Matt Hibner: ‘We’re Trying to Build a Family’ | Baltimore Ravens
text: Good. We were talking to Josh a few minutes ago. He said there's times where he goes to Darren and he's like, "Does this offense ever get easier?" How many times have you felt like that? And and what kind of keeps you sort of hopeful, invested in the offense, trying to get it mastered by the end. >> Yeah. Yeah. I mean, it sure it really is like kind of drinking from a fire hose for the first uh you know, we're actually still still a little bit like that, but um I think that's part of like the challenge that that our offense is trying to establish. And like Coach Doyle talks about like yeah, it's hard like we want to stress you guys, but also like we want to make it complex for us so that it's complex for defenses. You know, that's kind of the whole point. Um and we are starting to slow down a little bit with the install. So, it's coming and you know, just having reps being around the vets asking questions. Coach Gra does a great job of like hitting on certain points and and reviewing things in the meetings that you know maybe we should be touching on or or you know reviewing from practice. So um it's it's definitely uh it's definitely the most complex playbook I've ever tried or you know been in the process of learning but um it's it's coming along. >> Matt Mark tight ends. What's the culture and energy been like amongst you guys? What are you trying to build? >> Yeah. Uh I think we're just trying to build a family in the tight end room. Um, and I think that kind of expands to to to the offense and to the team as a whole. Um, but you know, it's just a bunch of great guys in the tight end room. Uh, I mean, Coach Graci, you know, he kind of sets the tone with that. Uh, he's he's an incredible coach. He really cares about us, you know, on the field, but also off the field, you know, as players, but also as people. Um, so just a ton of love and respect for him already. Um, and then Mark and Durham, you know, they really kind of lead the way, you know, as the older vets in the tight end room. Um, and everyone else, man, we're just we're all excited to be here, excited to be, you know, able to work with them and and learn from them, but also be around them off the field and spend time with them and get to know them as people, too. >> What stood out about Mark beyond what you already knew? I mean, accomplished player, all of that, but now getting to know him, getting to work with him the last few months, what what's kind of stood out maybe that you didn't realize? >> Yeah, I mean, I think just off the field, uh, you know, his character, uh, I think it just speaks volumes the way that, you know, he conducts his business. um you know, recovery, getting extra work in, you know, spending extra time with the coaches and and you know, really with with us as rookies. Um I just have a ton of respect for that and appreciation for it, too. Um but he he just operates like a true pro. So, it's it's super cool to be here, to be able to look up to him and how he does that and be able to learn from it. >> Matt, the last four years of your four games, I should say, of your college career in particular, watching you working with Jennings, I guess, seems like his elusiveness actually led to some nice big plays for you. talk about how you see Lamar Jackson. >> Yeah. Uh yeah, I've referenced that a couple of times. I mean, Lamar's obviously, you know, one of the freakiest athletes I've ever been around, ever seen. Um so his ability to extend plays and and scramble and make, you know, plays out of nothing is uh you know, just beyond impressive. And uh you know, in college at SMU, Kevin Jennings was pretty similar in that regard. Uh just being able to keep plays alive. Like you never go dead on the route. you're always scrambling to get open, staying staying a viable option for the quarterback because uh you know it's kind of just that trust factor and that chemistry that they're going to be able to make something happen and uh a lot of times they do just that. So it's uh it's mutually beneficial for sure. >> What can you get out of that? >> Yeah. Um, I think just being in in a pre, you know, in an NFL game one, like diving into that environment. Uh, you know, experiencing it firsthand. Um, being able to play against another team and experience that. Uh, you know, obviously we're going against the same defense every day. So, you kind of learn players and tendencies and things like that. So, uh, you know, being against a new opponent, being able to work things full speed from that regard. Um, and I think it's an advantage for the offense because our defense knows our offense so well at this point. Um, so we we get to run some some plays against new looks and see how they go. And and for me, it's all about just, you know, kind of seeing what that feels like, getting uh, you know, some reps underneath me in games. So that's what I'm looking forward to. Matt, >> that's a nice metal score you got on your neck there. Do you remember at what point in practice to pick that up? >> Uh, I mean, it could have been a few of them, but uh, you know, I think, uh, you know, we try to be physical and, uh, you know, I'm I'm doing my best to do that and, uh, I think it's great for the team, great for me. So, uh, yeah, there's a couple plays where some bigger collisions, but who knows? with the upper body. >> Yeah, I think right now it's it's all about putting me in different positions and seeing how I play and uh you know, trying to get me to learn both, be as complete of a player as I can so that I can do uh you know, whatever the offense needs me to do. Um, and uh, that's kind of really just the main focus for me right now. >> Uh, I mean, there's definitely a level up from there. Um, you know, every play is probably a little bit higher intensity. You know, there's a lot more, you know, athleticism on the field as a whole, but, uh, you know, football's football, so you just you try to level up as the game levels up. So, it's it's been it's been football. Thanks guys. >> Appreciate it.

title: Keary Colbert: ‘We Love What Zay Flowers Brings to the Table’ | Baltimore Ravens
text: Uh first off, just wanted to thank uh Mr. Bashaud and Coach Minner for the opportunity to be here. You know, excited about the season and um excited to meet you guys as well. So, open it up. >> Um Jacoby's just arguably the talk of camp uh for a for a guy who just got here. Um you know, what do you kind of see about him that has led him to make some of these dazzling catches so early in camp and with such consistency? >> Yeah, I mean, that's really been part of his DNA um really since he's come out of high school. Um myself, Prentice, we've been able to kind of get to know him for a number of years and if you really go back and just study, you know, him as a player from high school to college, I mean, he makes these plays or he's made these plays, you know, um in high school and college and um he's really just being himself. He's working hard. He's he's taking advantage of opportunities that come his way and um you know, he's a he's a talented receiver and and uh you know, he has a he has some really good hands and and um I'm excited about, you know, how he's performing, how the other guys are performing in the group. Um we have a really good room. Everybody's pushing one another and supporting one another and um it's been really fun to watch the group um as a whole. >> With the SoCal connection you have with him and the relationship you have going back, does it make you harder on him cuz you you know what to expect out of him? >> No, I wouldn't say that, but um you know, I would like to think that, you know, we're kind of we we're hard on on them all the same and we love on them the same way, you know what I mean? So, um but um of course, you know, I love that he's a Trojan and um I'm excited uh you know, about the opportunity to have him here in this organization and and um you know, we look forward to to him, you know, starting his career and and doing some great things. >> Very good. This has been an organization obviously has been very significant emphasis on the wide receiver blocking in particular. Talk about that maybe with with with X and and what that what that means to you and how important it is to emphasize that this group. >> Oh, yeah, it's very important. Um you know, I think that's a important aspect of the game, you know, to be a complete receiver. I think that's everybody's goal, you know, you know, you want to catch the ball but also you want to be involved in the in the run game as well. That's part of the job description. Um and we have a great group of guys that are that are invested in to being complete receivers and doing whatever it takes uh to help the offense and help the team and and um so, you know, I'm excited in that way to watch the guys compete to block, to catch, to run, to play special teams, do whatever we can to help this organization win. >> Obviously, last year Rashod Bateman didn't have the year that he wanted. Um what are your expectations or what what does a bounce back year look like for him in your eyes? What do you expect from him this season? >> Yeah, I'm excited for his opportunity to to have a great season. I mean, I think that's the great thing about a new season is that everything that happened in the past is behind you. You can learn from it and and I think he's excited about this next chapter, this next opportunity and and you know, I think he's had a great camp. He's had a great off season. Um he's been attentive. He's a smart player. He's you know, he he has a very high skill set from a receiver standpoint. Um you know, I'm excited about what he brings to the room and he's a pro's pro. Uh he comes about his work every day. He's out here every day. So, um I'm excited for for the year to come for him. >> There has been some discussion this off season about whether Zay Flowers is your number one receiver. Um just generally, how have you seen what people think of what they think number one wide receiver over the years and why do you think Zay fits that mold? >> I mean, as far as what, you know, outside people think it's all subjective, you know, everybody has uh different wants and needs and expectations but as far as us in in in this organization, you know, we love what he brings to the table from a from a skill set, from a mentality. Um he's positive energy every day. When he's in here, he's smiling. I mean, you guys know you guys have known him longer than me, but he's always smiling. He has a great uh energy about him. He loves football. He loves to compete. He wants to do whatever it takes to win. Um so, I think, you know, that's the the best thing about him and and um I think that uh you know, he's he's helping lead our group, you know, being more vocal uh in that role. So, you know, he's a he's a great leader. He leads by example, but at the same time, he'll get the guys going. Uh he'll he supports the boys in the room, you know, so it's been fun to be around him and watch him uh be out there on the grass and um you know, his skill set is is is tremendous. >> Okay. Yeah, the the knock on Jakobi coming into the league from some analysts was just like a lack of separation, but what have you seen in camp and then on digs, come back and watch a bunch of different routes. Do you think he has improved kind of like from the mental side of the game to understanding how to attack leverages? Is it Is it more, you know, the game speed's slowing down for him where he's able to to get open more easily? I mean, where have you kind of seen him take the biggest leap as a route runner? >> Yeah, I think the longer he's here, um the slower the game will be. That's for any rookie. That's for Elijah. That's for any of the young guys in the room at the end of the day. Like, um you know, there is a transition from college to pro and and uh I think he's transitioning in very well. Um I know he's working really hard to learn and and grow and watch tape and understand, you know, the the different nuances of the offense or or the schemes on defense or the players he's playing against. So, um you know, at the end of the day, like he's a sponge and he's continuing to get better every day, which is all that we hope for at this point and and uh we'll see where that takes him. But, I think uh you know, he's doing a great job and um I I continue to to to be encouraged by how he's working and and and what his future will potentially look like. >> You and Declan what was it like game prepping and game planning against Jesse the past couple years and what was your initial reaction when he reached out to to bring you over here? >> Yeah, I mean it was tough. I mean he's multiple on defense. He you know, he had a bunch of guys and that that played hard. I think that was probably the the biggest thing that we knew is like they were going to play a certain style of of football. They're tough and and you know, he he's multiple and and how he presents his defense. So it was fun and you know, I actually work with Jesse way back in the day at Georgia State. So I've kind of gone against him you know before and for a number of years but you know, I just love how he presents his defense and and how he gets his guys going and and it's it's showing out here on this field too. Like I love competing against these guys and you know, between him and coach Weave and that whole defensive staff like they got those guys flying around. It's iron sharpening iron. You know, our guys are are you know, up for the challenge every day and it's really been fun watching these guys compete in practice every day. >> You and Declan both coached under Sean Payton. Declan you know, coached under Sean Payton for a long time. I know he has a bunch of influences. He's his own guy but are there certain mannerisms, characteristics of Declan where you're like, okay, that's from Sean or is there anything >> You know what? I've been around Declan and and I wouldn't say that and I mean me. I mean he might say that. I would just say like from what I've known for Declan or being around Declan like he's always been the same guy. Like to be honest like when I was when we were at the previous place working if I had any questions in the offense on the field or anything like that, I would literally ask Declan. You know what I mean? So he's very detailed. The same things that he preaches to our to our offense or offensive staff, you know, detailed and and and just having an emotion and and passion and energy and going out there and playing the game the right way. Um you know, that's that's him every day. And whether he's a coordinator, whether he's a position coach, that's just the type of person he is. And um but but I would say like he's very detailed and and um you know, he's very smart and and he's doing a great job of just leading the offense and and setting us in the right direction. >> Keary, Rashod said the other day that he feels like in this offense he can be less one-dimensional. I guess how do you think kind of that lack of rigidity in his game for us now is going to make the most of what he can do on the field? >> Yeah, I mean, I think uh he has a good opportunity just like the other guys. I mean, Declan is going to move pieces around, move people around and and um that's the fun part about this offense at this point is that we're still trying to figure out how it's going to fit and and the pieces are going to fit and how to use certain people in certain packages and um but right now I think everybody's doing a great job of just attacking the day and attacking whatever opportunity comes their way. Um and and you know, like I said earlier like kind of led by some of the older guys. Bate and Zay, you know, they kind of they set the the kind of the the mentality for the room and they come out every day and everybody just kind of goes off of them and we just we just worry about the day and worry about the opportunities when they come and then we'll kind of add it up at the end. >> Two more? >> Keary, Jessie described Prentice Gill as a rising star in the industry. How do you guys kind of see him as an asset to you and your room? >> Man, um I've been fortunate to know Prentice for a long time and you know, one of my very close friends and and he's a guy that I've worked with before in the past and even when we were coaching in different places, we always each year bouncing ideas off each other and and kind of talking ball one another. But uh to your point, very much an asset for me, for our staff, uh for our room. Um you know, obviously he's been here for a while. He has a great relationship with the guys in the room. He understands the guys in the room and kind of you know, the skill sets and and just little things about, you know, the the the players. Um but, you know, I do believe and and do agree that he's a rising star in the profession and you know, I'm fortunate and blessed to to have him um you know, as part of our group and and you know, he and I just kind of had net and and getting after it every single day, but you know, he's very smart. He works hard. He's detailed. Um so, I look forward to to continue to watch him, you know, and hopefully, you know, we're we're doing it here for a while, but um you know, when you get good coaches, man, you you got to always you know, at times, you know, they're they're probably going to leave at some point, but while he's here, man, we going to uh you know, we're going to do it well, do well together and and um I'm excited for him and and his career as he continues to to do well in the in the profession. >> Thanks, guys. >> Appreciate it. Yeah, appreciate it.

title: The Ravens' Tight End Situation Is Getting Concerning...
text: Two positions I'll give you Jerry and one of them is what Cole talked about. Uh tight end concerns me suddenly. And Hibner and Kvepis have made some plays. Hibner especially, I think he's come on. But I don't know, man. And Smythe is going to play a ton just by what we're seeing. I would give Darren Waller a call. I said that on the sideline. Get a big big ass red zone threat that you can throw the ball to and another weapon. I I I'm I don't know if he's obviously Dar- Darren's been up front about some of the things he's battled. I would eat obviously have to check in on where he is health-wise, mentally, physically with him. I would look around a little bit to see if you might be able to bring in another third down red zone kind of guy. And it's clear De'Angelo loves his tight ends. It's a lot to ask, man. Tight end's a hard position to make the transition to the NFL in a sophisticated offense. And we see some things every day. I mean, there's been way too many drops from the tight end position. Now, that'll probably that that includes Mark Andrews, who's probably been the leader in the that this off season. But um >> This Everyone's going to love hearing that, Joe. >> I know. I mean, you got to be honest. Look, I'm I'm not worried about it, but we're This is what we see. Dropped another one today. He put a ball on the ground yesterday, although it was so rainy and nasty that nobody could hold the ball. So, that that's a caveat there. But um I don't know. I I I think the young tight ends are coming along. But that's a lot to ask. Are they going to be ready to be meaningful uh contributors by the time the regular season rolls around? And building off what Cole said about the interior defensive line, I think at the very least, I think they need to get a body in here. I don't think they could play a preseason game with what they currently have on the field. They can, but they're going to be pushing big men in the heat way too far, and that's going to lead to injuries and and then that's just becomes a slippery slope. These guys are playing so many snaps. They look dead today some of their defensive lineman. Now, let us go through this guys. Um Peoples' undisclosed injury has missed two straight two or three straight practices. Madubuike is very early in his ramp up. He's not even doing individual stuff. He's basically warming up and doing conditioning. Calais Campbell still ramping up, not doing team stuff, is doing mostly conditioning and some uh individual stuff. Uh John Jenkins same as Broderick Washington, mostly conditioning, not taking part in team stuff quite yet. C.J. This is always difficult because you think about Coach Reid's process, it's all about pushing and pulling and really pushing the guys for three straight days in pads, which keep in mind guys had not been in pads all off season. But now you're back in pads today. How do you respond to that? And I mean it's hot out here. You could tell the guys are kind of going through it. It's 2 hours and 25 minutes. After a 10-10-10 no pads shells practice to come right back out after it. How do guys respond? Chamari Conner is now back uh in a safety position where he's facing the play. Last year he played a lot of slot. Uh kind of a hybrid safety slot corner position, but many times, depending on the coverage and depending on the scheme, he had to turn his back to the play or turn his hips or turn his shoulders.
